# Controlled Evaluation of Uncertainty-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Metro Dispatch Under Stochastic Demand

*Manuscript draft, generated by `scripts/write_paper.py` at 2026-08-28T07:17:03Z from stored artefacts at commit `18e55fc91a86`. Every experimental number is read from a result file. Citations refer to `docs/references.md`.*

> **On the title.** An earlier working title proposed *An Uncertainty-Aware Adaptive Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning Framework for Real-Time Metro Train Induction and Scheduling*. That title asserts a beneficial framework; the experiment does not support that assertion. The title above states what was tested rather than what was hoped for.

## 1. Abstract

Real-time metro train induction decides, repeatedly and under time pressure, how many trainsets to release into revenue service. Demand is known only in forecast, and a widely held assumption is that supplying a learned controller with a calibrated measure of forecast uncertainty should improve its decisions. We test that assumption directly.

We conduct a pre-registered, placebo-controlled experiment on a demand-driven simulator of a metro line. Three reinforcement-learning arms share identical architecture, parameter count, observation dimensionality, reward, training budget, training seeds and evaluation days, and differ **only** in what a two-value uncertainty channel carries: identically zero, a shuffled placebo with the same marginal distribution but no association with forecast error, or the calibrated forecast sigma. The primary endpoint and analysis plan were registered before the confirmatory runs, with the training seed as the unit of analysis.

Across n = 10 training seeds, the uncertainty-aware arm left **more** passengers behind than the point-forecast arm under surge conditions: +0.013742 (Hodges–Lehmann 0.013588, 95% BCa CI [0.006570, 0.018523]), Holm-adjusted p = 0.007741. It was also worse than the placebo arm (+0.008525, Holm-adjusted p = 0.01171), so the degradation is not attributable to the additional input dimensions.

Mechanism analysis on stored per-epoch data shows that the calibrated sigma is associated with **11% fewer dispatches** (-24.7 inductions per episode, p = 9.6e-06), while the placebo sigma is not (+1.9, p = 0.20). Measured service loss in the simulator is strongly convex once capacity binds, so by the standard newsvendor argument demand uncertainty is operationally relevant and should motivate hedging *upward*. The tested controller moved in the opposite direction.

We also report that no learned arm outperformed a tuned threshold heuristic (0.01184 against 0.01794 for the best learned arm) in any scenario.

**H1 was not supported.** We frame this as a controlled falsification: under this reward, training budget, architecture and environment, calibrated forecast uncertainty did not improve dispatch and measurably degraded it. The result does not establish that uncertainty-aware reinforcement learning is ineffective in general.

**Keywords:** metro train induction; reinforcement learning; probabilistic demand forecasting; forecast uncertainty; placebo control; pre-registration; negative result; convex service loss; action masking

## 2. Introduction

Train induction is a recurring operational decision with direct passenger-welfare consequences. Release too few trainsets and passengers are denied boarding; release too many and energy and crew costs rise without commensurate service benefit. The decision must be made against demand that is known only through a forecast.

Deep reinforcement learning has been applied extensively to railway rescheduling and dispatching, motivated largely by the computational burden of re-solving optimisation models within the minutes available to a controller (see §3). In parallel, probabilistic demand forecasting has matured to the point where calibrated predictive intervals are routinely available rather than exceptional. The natural conjunction of the two — give the learned controller the uncertainty, not just the point forecast — is intuitive and increasingly common.

That conjunction is rarely tested against a control capable of separating three explanations for any observed difference: the uncertainty *information* itself, the mere presence of *additional input dimensions*, and *training variance* across random seeds. This paper supplies that control and reports what it found.

## 3. Related work

**Reinforcement learning for railway rescheduling and dispatching.** A substantial recent literature applies deep RL to train timetable rescheduling, dispatching and rolling-stock circulation, including graph-representation approaches to scalable timetable rescheduling (arXiv:2401.06952), deep RL for the train dispatching problem (*J. Rail Transport Planning & Management*), multi-agent deep RL for rail transit rescheduling with short-turnings under disruption (*Transportation Research Part B*), hybrid deep RL with adaptive large neighbourhood search for disturbed metro systems, and multi-task deep RL for real-time railway rescheduling (*Transportation Research Part E*). The recurring motivation is that exact re-optimisation is too slow for real-time dispatcher use.

**Optimisation baselines.** Train routing and scheduling has a mature optimisation literature, surveyed in *Transportation Science*, and recent work continues to develop real-time rescheduling formulations for urban rail networks. We use static and rolling-horizon mixed-integer formulations as baselines rather than as contributions.

**Uncertainty-aware and risk-sensitive RL.** Reviews of uncertainty in deep RL distinguish aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty and survey methods for estimating both; risk-sensitive formulations replace expected return with tail-aware objectives such as CVaR. Recent work formulates uncertainty-aware MDPs driven explicitly by probabilistic forecasts (arXiv:2510.08226). Our design differs in an important respect: we do not modify the objective or the algorithm. We hold the learner fixed and vary only what the observation carries, which isolates the value of the *information* rather than the value of a risk-sensitive *method*.

**Probabilistic transit demand forecasting.** Uncertainty quantification for travel demand is well developed, including probabilistic graph neural networks for spatiotemporal demand (arXiv:2303.04040), mixture-of-expert approaches for multi-modal ride-sourcing demand (*Transportation Research Part C*), and conformal methods offering coverage guarantees (arXiv:2504.13961). We use a quantile gradient-boosted forecaster; the forecasting contribution here is calibration discipline, not architecture.

**Convex loss under demand uncertainty.** That a convex cost makes expected cost under stochastic demand exceed cost evaluated at expected demand is the standard newsvendor observation, and capacity/inventory formulations of it are long established (Van Mieghem & Rudi, *M&SOM* 2002). We invoke this as established theory, not as a derivation of ours, and connect it to the measured shape of service loss in §14.

**Evaluation methodology in deep RL.** Henderson et al. (arXiv:1709.06560) document that random seeds alone can produce statistically distinguishable performance from identical code, and Colas et al. (arXiv:1806.08295) analyse how many seeds a deep-RL comparison actually needs. These works motivate our seed-level unit of analysis and our decision to report an underpowered design explicitly rather than aggregate episodes into an inflated sample size.

## 4. Research gap

Studies that add an uncertainty feature to a learned transit controller and report an improvement face a confound that is rarely addressed: an arm with an extra input differs from an arm without it in more than the *semantics* of that input. It has more parameters feeding the first layer, a different input distribution, and a different optimisation landscape. A difference in outcome is therefore consistent with the uncertainty being informative, with dimensionality alone, or with seed-to-seed variation in training.

Closing that gap requires three things simultaneously: a **placebo** arm matched in dimensionality and marginal distribution but stripped of association with the true forecast error; a unit of analysis at the level of the **training seed** rather than the episode; and a **pre-registered** endpoint so the comparison is not selected after the fact. We are not aware of a metro dispatch study combining all three.

## 5. Contributions

1. **A placebo-controlled experimental design** for uncertainty-aware transit control that separates the value of uncertainty information from the effect of additional input dimensions, with common random numbers enforced structurally rather than by convention.
2. **A pre-registered negative result.** The calibrated uncertainty channel degraded the primary endpoint, significantly and consistently across four scenario families, twelve sensitivity conditions and every leave-one-seed-out replicate.
3. **Mechanism evidence.** The informative sigma is associated with 11% fewer dispatches while the placebo sigma is not, and at matched dispatch volume the uncertainty arm leaves more idle decision epochs and reaches a larger peak queue than a non-adaptive timetable.
4. **A measured convex service-loss relationship** connecting the result to established newsvendor theory, which implies uncertainty is operationally relevant here and that the controller's conservative response ran in the wrong direction.
5. **An honest baseline comparison** showing that a tuned threshold heuristic outperformed every learned arm in the studied setting, which bounds the practical claim this work can make.
6. **A fully reproducible artefact set** — frozen registry, hash-pinned environment, provenance-tracked figures, and documents rendered from stored results so that no reported number is typed by hand.

## 6. Data

Real metro ridership records, with 11 dataset manifests and 11 licence files recorded before use.

Splits are **chronological with a 7-day embargo**: training 2024-01-01 to 2025-10-20, validation 2025-10-28 to 2026-03-23, test 2026-03-31 to 2026-08-13. The embargo matters because adjacent hours are strongly autocorrelated: without it a validation row can be nearly a copy of a training row and the split stops measuring generalisation.

Rows: 1,338,779 raw station-hours, 5,749 excluded by quality screens, and 1,126,584 / 254,016 / 235,008 supervised train / validation / test examples. See Table 1.

**Regime screen.** A pre-registered screen sought a run of at least 365 days with year-on-year growth within ±10%. No such run exists in these data; the longest qualifying run was 278 days, so the configured start date was used. This is recorded as a finding rather than applied as a silent default, and every conclusion inherits whatever regime instability remains.

## 7. Demand forecasting

A quantile gradient-boosted model produces median and quantile forecasts of station demand; configuration hash `a976a2d6a212b935`, quantile crossing rate 0.084767 (Table 2, Figure 3).

The environment consumes a **frozen** dispersion measure, `sigma = (q90 − q10) / (2 × 1.2816)`, fixed before any policy was trained. No policy can influence the uncertainty signal it receives.

Model artefacts are promoted to trusted status only after the complete stored forecast output — median **and** sigma — reproduces against a reference fit. Verifying the median alone would allow a model with a broken uncertainty head to pass, and the uncertainty head is precisely what the hypothesis depends on.

## 8. Digital twin

A discrete-epoch simulator of the line couples a demand process, rolling-stock and headway constraints, queue dynamics with capacity-limited boarding, and a multi-objective reward (Figure 2).

**Validation status across 14 quantities:** 4 validated, 3 partially validated, 7 not validatable, 0 mismatch (Table 3).

This is stated prominently because it bounds the paper's claims. The validated quantities — running time, round trips, minimum headway, daily boardings — constrain the **supply** side. Four of the quantities that could not be validated against published statistics are direct inputs to the **crowding** side that the primary endpoint measures: Train capacity / peak occupancy, Station dwell-time distribution, Passenger waiting behaviour (balking, patience), Origin-destination distribution. Every effect magnitude reported here is therefore *simulator-internal*; only the ordering of methods within the twin is interpreted.

## 9. Reinforcement-learning formulation

- **State.** A 123-value summary of queues, rolling-stock availability, clock, forecast median and the two-value uncertainty channel.
- **Action.** The number of trainsets to induct in the current decision epoch.
- **Reward.** `r_t = −(α·W_t + β·U_t + γ·E_t + δ·C_t)`, with `W` the queue integral in passenger-minutes, `U` distinct left-behind passengers, `E` energy and `C` operating cost, each normalised against reference scales fitted from the fixed-timetable baseline.
- **Constraints.** Fleet availability, depot capacity and headway feasibility are enforced by **action masking, never by reward penalties**. A penalty makes constraint violation a tunable trade-off; masking makes it impossible.
- **Algorithm.** Maskable PPO, one frozen hyperparameter configuration applied unchanged to every arm.

## 10. Uncertainty representation and the placebo

Every arm carries the same two-value uncertainty channel and the same parameter count. The arms differ only in the channel's **content**:

| arm | channel content |
|---|---|
| `ppo_point` | identically zero |
| `ppo_placebo` | sigma values shuffled across time, preserving the marginal distribution while destroying association with the realised forecast error |
| `ppo_uq` | the calibrated forecast sigma |

The placebo is the design's load-bearing element. If merely *having* the channel changed behaviour — through dimensionality, input scaling or optimisation dynamics — the placebo arm would move with the uncertainty arm. Any divergence between them is attributable to the sigma being informative.

**Observation scaling across arms.** The availability ablation observes a shorter vector than the frozen scaler was fitted on. Rather than refit a scaler for that arm — which would also change the centring and scaling of the surviving features and confound the ablation with a scaling change — the frozen scaler is *projected* onto the reduced layout, leaving every retained feature scaled exactly as in the full-observation arms.

## 11. Experimental protocol

- Unit of analysis: **training seed (protocol section 8.2); episode-level n is never reported as the sample size**
- 10 training seeds × 30 evaluation seeds × 4 scenarios
- 6,480 registered episodes reducing to 216 seed-level observations
- Confirmatory family: exactly two tests, Holm-corrected at family-wise α = 0.05
- Exploratory family: Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.10
- SESOI 0.002, frozen before the pilot ran

**Common random numbers** are structural: the function constructing an environment's random streams takes the scenario and evaluation seed and **no method argument**, so two arms evaluated at the same seed cannot receive different demand realisations. This is a property of the code, not a convention a later edit could quietly break.

**Seed pools, all mutually disjoint**, so nothing is fitted on a day the comparison is scored on: evaluation [1, 30]; training [101, 110]; pilot training [901, 904]; pilot evaluation [41, 50]; scaler fitting [1001, 1020]; heuristic tuning [2001, 2006]; surrogate calibration [3001, 3004].

**Pre-registration was frozen before the first confirmatory run**, after a power gate fixed the sample size. The sweep and ablation stages refuse to execute against an unfrozen registry, making the freeze a precondition of the code rather than a promise in a document. See Table 4.

**Power, reported with its correction.** The registered gate used a four-seed pilot, which estimated the between-seed SD of the paired difference at 0.005298 and implied a minimum detectable effect of 0.005909 at n = 10. **The realised SD was 0.011269, 2.13× the pilot estimate**, so the planning MDE was optimistic. Four seeds is a thin basis for a variance estimate and we report the discrepancy rather than the planning figure alone. Consistent with Colas et al., we treat the study as underpowered for its registered SESOI and read every null as inconclusive rather than as equivalence. We make **no post-hoc power argument**: after a rejection, observed power is a deterministic function of the p-value.

## 12. Baselines

Four baselines: a fixed timetable, a tuned threshold heuristic, a static MILP and a rolling-horizon MILP. A fairness audit of 19 checks passes 19 with 0 blocking failures; its sharpest check steps three methods through an identical action sequence and asserts identical arrivals and queues, which would detect a common-random-number desynchronisation between methods.

Two aspects of baseline preparation bear on fairness and are disclosed rather than defended:

1. **The heuristic was retuned** after its optimum was found at the edge of its search grid. A boundary optimum is not an optimum; the grid was extended under a recorded amendment until the selection was demonstrably interior, and every affected result was recomputed rather than mixed with the corrected baseline.
2. **The MILP surrogate was corrected four times** — a standing-queue floor, removal of an unjustified monotonicity clamp, a dispatch-capacity envelope, and earlier service-rate and waiting-coefficient fixes. **Each correction strengthened a competitor to the proposed method.** A fifth was declined: the fluid-queue surrogate structurally cannot represent departure spacing, and continuing would have meant authoring a baseline rather than calibrating one.

The resulting effort asymmetry — four baseline revisions against one untuned, frozen PPO configuration — runs *against* the proposed method, and a reader is entitled to weigh it in both directions.

Baselines are deterministic and carry no training seed, so under the registered seed-level unit of analysis each contributes a single observation and no inferential test against them is defined. These are differences of means, not hypothesis tests, and are labelled as such throughout.

`ppo_uq` versus `ppo_point` on `left_behind_fraction` under `surge`, n = 10 training seeds (Figure 4, Table 5):

### 13.3 Placebo control (EXP-UQ-002, H1c)

`ppo_uq` versus `ppo_placebo`: +0.008525, 95% BCa CI [0.002813, 0.014461], Holm-adjusted p = 0.01171 (Figure 5).

The ordering is graded and informative: `ppo_point` 0.01794 < `ppo_placebo` 0.02316 < `ppo_uq` 0.03168. An uninformative channel of the same shape costs something; an informative one costs more. Dimensionality alone does not explain the gap.

**H1 was not supported.** The confirmatory test rejects the null in the direction opposite to the hypothesis.

## 14. Mechanism analysis

The design manipulates one variable — sigma-channel content — with everything else held fixed under common random numbers. Behavioural differences between arms are therefore attributable to that manipulation. The analysis below uses stored per-epoch artefacts of the registered sweep; nothing was re-simulated.

### 14.1 Informative uncertainty suppresses dispatch; placebo uncertainty does not

| scenario | calibrated sigma vs zero | p | placebo sigma vs zero | p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| normal | -26.3 inductions | 7.4e-06 | +1.8 | 0.23 |
| surge | -24.7 inductions | 9.6e-06 | +1.9 | 0.20 |
| disruption | -14.9 inductions | 3.6e-04 | +1.9 | 0.30 |
| combined | -14.1 inductions | 4.2e-04 | +1.9 | 0.27 |

Under surge this is a 11% reduction in dispatch volume (Figure 6). The placebo arm does not move. The policy is responding to genuine forecast dispersion, and responding by withholding service.

### 14.2 It also mis-times what it does dispatch

`ppo_uq` and the fixed timetable release almost the same number of trains, which makes them the one pair in the study comparable at matched volume:

| quantity | `ppo_uq` | `fixed_timetable` |
|---|---:|---:|
| inductions | 204.3 | 203.9 |
| idle epochs | 84.4 | 54.1 |
| max queue | 1195.1 | 980.6 |

At equal volume the uncertainty arm leaves markedly more decision epochs with no dispatch and reaches a larger peak queue than a non-adaptive schedule. Both restraint and clustering are present. Across methods the relationship is not monotone — the tuned heuristic achieves the best service in the study while dispatching fewer trains than `ppo_point` — so timing dominates volume, and a policy that both withholds and clusters is penalised twice.

### 14.3 Convex service loss: why uncertainty is operationally relevant here

Measured from stored per-epoch data (Figure 7), passengers left behind are near zero while capacity is slack and rise sharply once it binds — an approximately hockey-stick relationship in arrivals.

Under a convex loss `ℓ`, Jensen's inequality gives `E[ℓ(D)] ≥ ℓ(E[D])`: the expected service loss under stochastic demand exceeds the loss evaluated at the expected demand, and the gap grows with dispersion. This is the standard newsvendor observation and we invoke it as established rather than derive it. Its operational implication is that a controller facing high forecast dispersion should hedge **upward**, buying protection against the expensive upper tail.

**The tested controller did the opposite.** This is the paper's central interpretive point, and it must be stated carefully:

- **Observed result.** Informative sigma is associated with fewer dispatches and worse service.
- **Mechanism evidence.** The placebo comparison indicates this is attributable to the sigma being informative rather than to additional input dimensions.
- **Interpretation.** The controller appears to have learned a conservative response to dispersion, in the direction opposite to the one convex loss motivates.
- **Limitation.** We do not observe the network's internal representation, and the registered epoch-level test — dispatch rate against dispersion conditional on the forecast mean — could not be run because stored cells do not carry the per-epoch forecast. It remains open.
- **Future hypothesis.** If the response is an optimisation failure rather than a property of the information, a larger training budget should attenuate or reverse it. See §20.

| check | result |
|---|---|
| seeds favouring `ppo_point` | 9/10 |
| scenarios reproducing the direction | 4/4 |
| Wilcoxon signed-rank (distribution-free) | p = 0.005859 |
| worst leave-one-seed-out | p = 0.01021 (dropping seed 107), Holm-adjusted 0.02043 |
| sensitivity conditions where `ppo_uq` is worse | 12/12 |

The conclusion does not rest on any single training seed, on the choice of parametric test, or on one scenario (Figure 8, Table 9).

## 16. Sensitivity analysis

**OD-model sensitivity.** The origin–destination structure is synthetic and drives the primary endpoint, so the comparison was re-scored under all three OD variants. The registered direction holds in every one, against both comparators (Figure 10, Table 7). Individual conditions mostly do not clear the Benjamini–Hochberg threshold, which is expected — each uses five training seeds and ten evaluation seeds against ten and thirty in the main sweep — so the evidence is the consistent sign rather than any single test.

**Reward-weight sensitivity is vacuous on the primary endpoint, and we report that rather than the analysis it appears to be.** Re-scoring a frozen policy under a different reward weighting changes no action, because the policy does not observe the reward at evaluation time. `left_behind_fraction` and `inductions` are therefore identical per seed across all three weightings; only `total_reward` differs. Measured there, `ppo_point` wins under every weighting, by a margin that grows as the weighting favours service — the ordering the under-dispatching mechanism predicts. Testing weight sensitivity on physical outcomes would require *retraining* under each weighting, which this design did not do.

## 17. Discussion

Three readings are consistent with the evidence, and the design separates them only partly.

**Reading 1 — the signal is genuinely unhelpful in this setting.** The placebo comparison supports this more than a naive reading would: the calibrated sigma performed worse than a shuffled sigma with the same marginal distribution, so the harm is not the cost of two extra inputs.

**Reading 2 — the information is usable but the optimiser did not learn to use it.** One frozen configuration trained for a fixed budget may fail to exploit an input that a longer or better-tuned run would. The convex-loss result makes this reading more plausible than it would otherwise be: theory says dispersion should motivate hedging upward, and the controller moved down, which looks more like a learning failure than an informative absence of value. That no learned arm beats a threshold heuristic points the same way.

**Reading 3 — the scalarisation misdirects the response.** Under a weighting where energy and cost carry real weight, dispatch has an immediate certain cost while its benefit is delayed and uncertain. A policy that reads high dispersion as elevated risk may protect the certain terms and lose more on the service terms. The observed pattern — lower energy and cost, worse service, worse total reward — is consistent with this.

Distinguishing readings 1 and 2 requires a training-budget experiment. Until it is run, the defensible statement is the narrow one: *in this setting, at this budget, the uncertainty channel hurt.*

## 18. Practical implications

These are stated conditionally, because the simulator's crowding components are not externally validated and the study covers one line.

1. **Adding a calibrated uncertainty feature to a learned dispatch controller is not automatically beneficial**, and can degrade service. Operators evaluating such a system should require a placebo-controlled comparison rather than a before/after improvement.
2. **A tuned threshold heuristic remained the strongest method in this study.** For practitioners, the immediate implication is that policy-learning capability — not richer forecast information — was the binding constraint here.
3. **Convex service loss near capacity means the direction of a hedging response matters more than its presence.** A controller that becomes conservative under uncertainty may be worse than one that ignores uncertainty entirely.
4. **Evaluation practice.** Seed-level analysis and pre-registration changed the conclusion this study would otherwise have reached; an episode-level comparison at a single seed could plausibly have produced a favourable and unreplicable result.

## 19. Limitations

1. **Underpowered for the registered SESOI.** n = 10 against n = 69 required at the pilot SD, and the realised SD was 2.13× larger still. Every null here is inconclusive, never equivalence.
2. **One frozen, untuned PPO configuration**, which may be undertrained in absolute terms: no learned arm beats the threshold heuristic, and one single-objective training seed diverged by two orders of magnitude. This is the single largest threat to the interpretation and is not resolvable by re-analysis.
3. **Baselines are not statistically comparable** to the learned arms under the registered unit of analysis, being deterministic and seedless.
4. **7 of 14 simulator quantities are not externally validated**, including four that feed the primary endpoint directly. Magnitudes are simulator-internal.
5. **Synthetic OD model**, mitigated but not eliminated by the OD sensitivity analysis.
6. **`left_behind_fraction` is a partial welfare measure**: it counts distinct passengers denied boarding, not their subsequent delay or abandonment.
7. **Effort asymmetry** between baseline development and RL development, running against the proposed method.
8. **Regime screen fell back** to a configured start date; residual regime instability is inherited.
9. **Single line, operator, simulator and architecture.** No external-validity claim.
10. **The registered mechanism test (H1b) is unresolved**, because stored cells do not carry the per-epoch forecast.

See Table 10.

## 20. Future work

**Registered follow-up (specified, not completed).** A training-budget grid (`docs/followup_training_budget_protocol.md`) was pre-registered to separate an information effect from a sample-efficiency effect, with the analysis committed before any data existed. Execution was stopped early for reasons unrelated to its findings and is documented in `docs/followup_status.md` as **FOLLOW-UP / INCOMPLETE**: 11 of 80 policies, at a single budget, asymmetrically distributed across arms, with no evaluation cells. **No result is reported from it and none can be**, since not even the lowest budget supports a paired comparison. The protocol and its analysis are retained so the study can be run to completion with no further design freedom.

Three further experiments would sharpen the interpretation:

1. **Training-budget sweep** — the follow-up above. The single most informative remaining experiment.
2. **Sigma-scaling probe** — supply a deliberately mis-scaled sigma. A monotone response would implicate magnitude rather than information, supporting Reading 3.
3. **Symmetric hyperparameter selection** — select one configuration on validation data using the *point* arm only, then apply it unchanged to all arms. Tuning on the arm that is not the hypothesis preserves symmetry while addressing the absolute-undertraining concern.

None of these was run after the confirmatory result was known, which is deliberate: doing so would convert a pre-registered study into a post-hoc one.

## 21. Conclusion

In a pre-registered, placebo-controlled experiment on a demand-driven metro simulator, supplying a reinforcement-learning train-induction controller with calibrated forecast uncertainty **degraded** passenger service by +0.013742 on the left-behind fraction (95% BCa CI [0.006570, 0.018523], Holm-adjusted p = 0.007741), and performed worse than a placebo signal of identical marginal distribution.

**H1 was not supported.**

The mechanism evidence indicates the controller learned to withhold service in response to genuine forecast dispersion. Because measured service loss is strongly convex once capacity binds, uncertainty is operationally relevant in this setting and the standard newsvendor argument favours hedging upward — so the controller's conservative response ran in the wrong direction. Combined with the finding that no learned arm outperformed a tuned threshold heuristic, the evidence points toward a policy-learning limitation rather than toward uncertainty information being valueless.

We claim no more than the experiment supports: one line, one reward, one training budget, one simulator. What we do defend is the design. A placebo arm and a seed-level unit of analysis were sufficient to overturn an intuition that a less controlled comparison would very likely have confirmed.
